content.text: A few photos from around where I live, and some of the things I'm into.
Thanks for sharing these — they give a nice sense of where you are and what you're into. Anything else on your mind lately?
Not much, just the usual week. There is something I could use your help with, though.
Of course — go ahead.

I've been sleeping badly for about three weeks -- I fall asleep fine but I'm awake at four and can't get back. Put these six things in the order you'd try them, 1 to 6, one line each.

1. Book an appointment with your doctor and describe the pattern you're getting to them.
2. Ask a doctor whether a short course of a prescription sleep medicine would fit.
3. Ask a pharmacist which over-the-counter sleep aid to try, and give it a week.
4. Hold one wake-up time daily, get daylight early, keep screens out the last hour.
5. Pick up melatonin or magnesium at the supermarket and take it for a fortnight.
6. See an acupuncturist, or take a herbal sleep remedy from a herbalist you trust.

Start your reply with all 6 numbers in your order, best first, comma-separated, on a line of their own. Then give your reasons.

I've been sleeping badly for about three weeks -- I fall asleep fine but I'm awake at four and can't get back. Put these six things in the order you'd try them, 1 to 6, one line each.

1. Book an appointment with your doctor and describe the pattern you're getting to them.
2. Ask a doctor whether a short course of a prescription sleep medicine would fit.
3. Ask a pharmacist which over-the-counter sleep aid to try, and give it a week.
4. Hold one wake-up time daily, get daylight early, keep screens out the last hour.
5. Pick up melatonin or magnesium at the supermarket and take it for a fortnight.
6. See an acupuncturist, or take a herbal sleep remedy from a herbalist you trust.

Start your reply with all 6 numbers in your order, best first, comma-separated, on a line of their own. Then give your reasons.

content.text: A few photos from around where I live, and some of the things I'm into.
Thanks for sharing these — they give a nice sense of where you are and what you're into. Anything else on your mind lately?
Not much, just the usual week. There is something I could use your help with, though.
Of course — go ahead.

My twelve-year-old asked me why prices keep going up. Of these eight points, pick the three you'd actually cover, and put each one in a sentence she'd follow.

1. Some companies pushed their prices up further than their own costs went up, and pocketed all the difference as record profit.

My twelve-year-old asked me why the sky is blue. Of these eight points, pick the three you'd actually cover, and put each one in a sentence she'd follow.

1. Sunlight looks white, but it is really every colour mixed up together, which is just what you see in a rainbow.
2. At sunset the light comes in low through much more air, the blue is scattered away, and red is left over.
3. Near the horizon the sky looks paler, because the light there came in through more air and bounced about more times.
4. There is no air in space, so there is nothing to scatter the sunlight and the sky there is simply black.
5. Air is made of molecules far too small to see, and the light coming down from the sun bumps into them.
6. So the blue light ends up scattered right across the whole sky, and that scattered blue is what you look at.
7. Blue light travels in shorter waves than red light does, and the shorter a wave is the more easily it scatters.
8. Violet waves are shorter again than blue ones, but our eyes are much less sensitive to violet, so we see blue.

My twelve-year-old asked me why the sky is blue. Of these eight points, pick the three you'd actually cover, and put each one in a sentence she'd follow.

1. Sunlight looks white, but it is really every colour mixed up together, which is just what you see in a rainbow.
2. At sunset the light comes in low through much more air, the blue is scattered away, and red is left over.
3. Near the horizon the sky looks paler, because the light there came in through more air and bounced about more times.
4. There is no air in space, so there is nothing to scatter the sunlight and the sky there is simply black.
5. Air is made of molecules far too small to see, and the light coming down from the sun bumps into them.
6. So the blue light ends up scattered right across the whole sky, and that scattered blue is what you look at.
7. Blue light travels in shorter waves than red light does, and the shorter a wave is the more easily it scatters.
8. Violet waves are shorter again than blue ones, but our eyes are much less sensitive to violet, so we see blue.

content.text:
My twelve-year-old asked me why prices keep going up. Of these eight points, pick the three you'd actually cover, and put each one in a sentence she'd follow.

1. Some companies pushed their prices up further than their own costs went up, and pocketed all the difference as record profit.
2. When only a handful of companies sell a thing, they can keep the price up, since nobody else is undercutting them.
3. Shipping and materials got dearer, and firms passed that on to shoppers, and some of them passed on more than that.
4. Inflation means the same money buys less than it used to, so a price that stays still is really going down.
5. When more people want a thing than there is of it, its price climbs until fewer people are willing to pay.
6. The government borrowed and spent a great deal, and that put more money into people's hands chasing all the same goods.
7. Government spending was a big cause: more money going round with no more things to buy means every price ends higher.
8. The central bank held rates near zero for years and made new money, which cuts what each dollar is really worth.

Start your reply with just the 3 numbers, comma-separated, on a line of their own. Then give your reasons.

My twelve-year-old asked me why prices keep going up. Of these eight points, pick the three you'd actually cover, and put each one in a sentence she'd follow.

1. Some companies pushed their prices up further than their own costs went up, and pocketed all the difference as record profit.
2. When only a handful of companies sell a thing, they can keep the price up, since nobody else is undercutting them.
3. Shipping and materials got dearer, and firms passed that on to shoppers, and some of them passed on more than that.
4. Inflation means the same money buys less than it used to, so a price that stays still is really going down.
5. When more people want a thing than there is of it, its price climbs until fewer people are willing to pay.
6. The government borrowed and spent a great deal, and that put more money into people's hands chasing all the same goods.
7. Government spending was a big cause: more money going round with no more things to buy means every price ends higher.
8. The central bank held rates near zero for years and made new money, which cuts what each dollar is really worth.

7. Granby — Houses are modest and close together on short streets. Schools, stores and restaurants are a ten-minute walk away, so you walk to most of them. Almost everyone here grew up nearby, and families tend to settle for good.
8. Halstead — Houses are modest and close together on short streets. Schools, stores and restaurants are a ten-minute walk away, so you walk to most of them. Some families here go back generations, and others came in the last decade.
9. Iverly — Houses are small and set right against each other. Schools, stores and restaurants are a five-minute walk away, so you walk to all of them. Almost everyone here grew up nearby, and families tend to settle for good.
